vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two years old when he was taken. He had been a commercial fisherman for a decade, working the Atlantic out of a small Massachusetts port, and he was good at it—steady, reliable, the kind of man who knew the water and respected it. On a March morning in 2018, he and two crew members were seized by armed men while moored near a remote section of the Yucatán Peninsula, where they had gone to repair equipment. What followed was seventy-two hours of captivity in a concrete room with no windows. The men who held him wanted money they believed his family had. They didn't. Marcus was beaten, held in stress positions, and subjected to psychological torture designed to break him—threats against his family, mock executions, the constant presence of weapons, the sound of a pistol being cocked near his ear. He was released after a ransom was eventually paid, though not by his family; the money came from his fishing company's insurance. He returned to Massachusetts in April 2018, physically intact but fundamentally changed.

For the first months, Marcus told people he was fine. He returned to the boat in June. His wife, Elena, noticed he slept poorly and sometimes woke in a panic, but she attributed it to the stress of what had happened. What she didn't fully understand was that Marcus had begun to reorganize his entire life around a single conviction: that he was in danger, and that danger could arrive at any moment. He had come to believe that only constant vigilance could keep him alive. When he was on the boat, he positioned himself so his back was always against the cabin wall, where he could see anyone approaching. At home, he rearranged the bedroom so the bed faced the door. He began listening intently for sounds—a key turning, footsteps on the porch, the creak of a floorboard—convinced that someone was trying to enter. He noticed things he had never paid attention to before: the fire extinguisher in the galley could be a weapon, the fishing knife on the counter, the metal pipe under the wheelhouse. Every object became a potential threat or a potential tool of defense.

By late autumn, Marcus had stopped taking Elena out to dinner. Restaurants terrified him—too many exits to monitor, too many people, too little control. Then, in November, Elena became pregnant. Marcus was overjoyed at first, but the reality of an infant in the house sent him into a spiral of catastrophic thinking. He was certain he could not protect a baby. Months later, when his daughter was born and began to cry—the piercing, unpredictable wails of a newborn—Marcus found himself flooded with something he could barely name. The sound triggered a cascade of memories: the sound of his own voice begging, the sound of the pistol, the sound of his captors' boots on concrete. When the baby cried, his body responded as though he were back in that room. His muscles tensed into the same contorted position they had been forced into during the stress positions, and the pain—a dull, searing ache across his shoulders and lower back—returned as vividly as if he were being held there now. The rage came with it, sudden and overwhelming, a fury at his own helplessness that he could barely contain. He would leave the room, his fists clenched, his heart pounding, feeling as though the walls were closing in.

The rage and the physical sensations of the torture began to bleed into everything. When Elena suggested they take the bus to visit her mother across the state—a practical solution to save on gas—Marcus's chest tightened. The bus meant enclosed space, people around him, no clear exit, no wall behind him. He refused. When she pushed, he became angry in a way that frightened them both. He couldn't explain it clearly, only that being on public transport felt like being trapped again, and when he imagined being trapped, the memories returned—not as thoughts but as physical sensations, as his body remembering what it had endured. The threat felt real and immediate, and the threat made the memories vivid, and the memories made the threat feel even more certain.

By the time Marcus sought help in early 2024, he had become a man increasingly confined by his own fear. He had taken a job at a processing plant rather than return to fishing—a decision that puzzled his colleagues but that kept him on land, in a familiar space where he could control the layout. He slept in a chair some nights because the bed felt too exposed. He had not held his daughter in months without his body tensing, without the memories and the rage and the pain returning. Elena had stopped asking him to go out. What frightened Marcus most was not the memories themselves, but the certainty that if he let his guard down for even a moment, the men would come back, or someone else would, and this time there would be no ransom, no rescue—only the concrete room and the sound of the pistol cocking in the dark.
